It gives up Poland, the Baltic provinces, Finland, Ukraine — territory holding a large part of the Empire's population, coal and grain. It is signed because there is no army left with which to decline it. The front that could not be held in 1915 without shells could not be held in 1918 without men, and the men walked home.-8MANPOWER ▾-8MUNITIONS ▾-2HOME STABILITY ▾Settled recordEast Prussia: entered after the concentration was complete. 1915: the salient was given up and the army kept. August 1915: the Grand Duke retained the supreme command. 1916: the other fronts attacked in support. March 1917: the front commanders declined to advise. June 1917: the offensive was refused. Autumn 1914: Galicia was reinforced. The Emperor at headquarters: the question did not arise. The Second Army, August 1914: left to press on. The Carpathians, March 1915: pressed on into the mountains. The Guards, summer 1916: kept in reserve. Romania: an army sent at once. The death penalty: not restored. The Kornilov affair: the dismissal refused, and the march collapsed. Przemysl, winter 1914: assaulted. Lodz, November 1914: the Silesian offensive pressed on. East Prussia, February 1915:
